lessons.title: Chance, probability scales and outcomes
lessons.summary: Describe likelihood from impossible to certain and list the outcomes of a single event.
lessons.objective: Describe likelihood from impossible to certain and list the outcomes of a single event.
lessons.before: If each object in a bag is equally likely to be picked, a colour with more objects has a larger chance.
lessons.ideas:
For the same trial, compare how many equally likely results give each event.

A probability can be a fraction, decimal or percentage between 0 and 1, or between 0% and 100% when written as a percentage.

An equal-sized sector on a fair spinner has the same chance as any other equal-sized sector.
lessons.method:
Use probability words only after checking the possible results.

Convert to the same form before comparing two probabilities.

Say what one trial means before listing results.
mistakes: Unlikely means a low chance. Impossible has chance zero.
A percentage probability above 100% cannot describe a chance.
Equal-looking labels do not make unequal-sized sectors equally likely.

examples.title: Comparing chances in one bag
examples.question:
A bag has 5 blue, 2 red and 2 gold beads. A bead is drawn at random.

  1. Which is more likely, blue or red?

    [2]

  2. Describe the chance of drawing a green bead using probability language.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Each bead has the same chance of being picked.

There are more blue beads.

Blue

(b) A missing colour has zero chance of being drawn.

It is impossible because there are no green beads in the bag.

examples.title: Putting probability on a scale
examples.question:
A bag has 200 tokens of the same size, of which 34 are blue. One token is chosen at random.

  1. Find the probability of choosing a blue token as a fraction.

    [2]

  2. Give the same probability as a percentage.

    [2]

  3. Give the probability as a decimal and check where it lies on the scale.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The fraction is \(\frac{34}{200}\).

Divide the top and bottom by 2, then simplify if possible.

\(\frac{17}{100}\).

(b) The fraction has a denominator of 100 before simplification.

\(17\) %.

(c) Divide the percentage by 100 to give the decimal.

0.17. This is strictly between 0 and 1.

examples.title: Counting the outcomes of a spinner
examples.question:
A fair spinner has 10 equal-sized sectors numbered 1 to 10. A class of 2 pupils takes turns spinning it once each.

  1. How many different outcomes are possible on one spin?

    [2]

  2. Explain why 'lands on 1' and 'lands on 2' are mutually exclusive on one spin.

    [2]

  3. Explain why each numbered outcome has the same chance.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The possible outcomes are all the sector numbers, one per sector.

\(10\).

(b) Only one numbered sector can be the outcome of a spin. If the pointer stops right on a line, agree in advance to spin again.

A single spin cannot have both results at the same time.

(c) Fairness and equal sector size both matter.

The fair spinner has equal-sized sectors and each number appears in exactly one sector.

lessons.title: Theoretical and experimental probability
lessons.summary: Find a theoretical probability and use recorded trials to estimate a chance.
lessons.objective: Find a theoretical probability and use recorded trials to estimate a chance.
lessons.before: First list or count all the equally likely outcomes. Highlight the ones that give the event.
lessons.ideas:
The theoretical chance is wanted outcomes divided by all equally likely outcomes.

The experimental probability is the number of recorded successes divided by the number of trials.

Use total successes divided by total trials when combining trials under the same conditions.
lessons.method:
Check that the answer lies on the scale from 0 to 1.

Keep a tally after every trial and check the tallies add to the stated total.

Repeat using the same rules. Compare the estimates and consider their sample sizes.
mistakes: Do not divide by just the unwanted outcomes.
A theoretical chance and an experimental estimate may differ, especially with few trials.
A simple average of two estimates can give unequal trial groups the same weight.

examples.title: Picking a coloured token
examples.question:
A jar holds 5 purple, 3 orange and 6 white tokens of the same size. One token is chosen at random.

  1. Find the probability of a purple token.

    [2]

  2. Find the probability of a token that is not orange.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) There are 14 tokens in total.

5 of them give the wanted result.

\(\frac{5}{14}\).

(b) Purple and white are both allowed, so there are 11 wanted tokens.

\(\frac{11}{14}\).

examples.title: Running a chance experiment
examples.question:
A pupil gets blue 5 times in 105 trials of a spinner.

  1. What is the experimental probability of blue?

    [2]

  2. Describe how to carry out a fair repeat experiment and record results.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The wanted count is 5.

The full trial count is 105.

\(\frac{1}{21}\).

(b) Agree what to do if the arrow stops on a boundary. Keep track of the total number of spins.

Compare your estimate with the first estimate.

Use the same spinner and spin it the same way each time. Give each colour a tally and add a mark after each spin.

examples.title: Combining two sets of trials
examples.question:
One class records 5 purple results in 170 spins. A second class uses the same spinner and records 4 purple results in 20 spins.

  1. Find the experimental probability of purple using both classes together.

    [2]

  2. Explain why the combined result can be more useful than an estimate from just one class.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Combine the successes to get 9.

Combine the trials to get 190.

\(\frac{9}{190}\).

(b) The estimate can still vary even when the spinner stays the same.

It uses more trials, so an unusual result from one small set has less effect.
